Outdated, missing or unfollowed process documentation (SOPs) leading to inconsistent execution and onboarding inefficiency.
Weak continuous-improvement culture and limited use of data analytics/automation, so known inefficiencies persist.
Slow risk and management reporting (manual data aggregation) delaying decisions and increasing the cost of assurance.

tests.title: End-to-end cycle-time and SLA analysis
tests.objective: Confirm whether core processes complete within defined cycle times/SLAs and identify delays and bottlenecks.
tests.procedure: For each function, obtain transaction timestamp data for Q2 2026 (loan application-to-disbursement; requisition-to-PO-to-payment; period-end close timeline; risk-report production cycle). Compute actual cycle times and stage durations, compare to defined SLAs/targets, and identify the slowest stages, outliers and queues. Map where time is lost and quantify backlog/ageing.
tests.controlTested: Process efficiency and SLA performance (timeliness/efficiency).
tests.population: All in-scope transactions/processes with start–end timestamps in Q2 2026 across the four functions.
tests.sampleBasis: 100% data analytics on cycle times where timestamp data exists; judgemental deep-dive on the slowest decile and aged/backlog items.

tests.title: Process mapping and bottleneck / non-value-add identification
tests.objective: Identify bottlenecks, non-value-adding steps, and unclear ownership in each end-to-end process.
tests.procedure: Develop or validate end-to-end process maps (narrative/flowchart) for a key process in each function. Apply lean analysis to classify each step as value-add, business-non-value-add, or waste. Identify bottlenecks, redundant approvals, wait states, and steps lacking clear ownership. Corroborate via walkthroughs and staff interviews.
tests.controlTested: Process design efficiency and ownership clarity (effectiveness/efficiency).
tests.population: Documented and observed process flows for selected core processes in each function.
tests.sampleBasis: Judgemental — one high-volume/high-impact process per function, mapped end-to-end.

tests.title: Automation and straight-through-processing assessment
tests.objective: Assess the level of automation/STP and identify manual, spreadsheet and re-keying effort that could be automated.
tests.procedure: For each function, inventory the systems used and identify steps performed manually, in spreadsheets, or on paper, and points where the same data is re-keyed across systems. Quantify manual effort (volume × time) and STP rates. Benchmark against available system capability and identify candidate automations (system config, RPA, integration).
tests.controlTested: Degree of automation and elimination of manual effort (efficiency).
tests.population: Process-step inventory and system landscape for the four functions in Q2 2026.
tests.sampleBasis: Full process-step inventory per selected process; judgemental quantification of the highest-effort manual tasks.

tests.title: Rework, error and exception analysis
tests.objective: Quantify rework, errors and exceptions and determine their root causes and efficiency cost.
tests.procedure: Extract exception/rejection/rework data for Q2 2026 (e.g. returned requisitions, failed three-way matches, mis-booked loans, reconciliation differences, re-run/restated reports). Calculate error/rework rates by process and team, perform root-cause analysis on the largest categories, and estimate rework effort/cost. Identify recurring, avoidable causes.
tests.controlTested: First-time-right / rework rate (quality/efficiency).
tests.population: Exception, rejection, error and rework logs across the four functions for Q2 2026.
tests.sampleBasis: 100% analytics on available exception data; judgemental root-cause sampling of top error categories.

tests.title: Handoff and cross-functional friction review
tests.objective: Confirm handoffs between Credit, Procurement, Finance and Risk are timely, clear and free of duplication.
tests.procedure: Map key inter-function handoffs (e.g. credit disbursement-to-finance posting; procurement-to-AP/finance; risk data-to-credit and risk-to-finance reporting). For a sample, measure handoff lag, identify data re-entry, reconciliation breaks and disputes over ownership, and assess SLAs between functions. Interview both sides of each handoff.
tests.controlTested: Efficiency and clarity of cross-functional handoffs (process integration).
tests.population: Inter-function handoff transactions and interfaces in Q2 2026.
tests.sampleBasis: Judgemental sample of the principal handoffs between each pair of functions, with timing analysis.

tests.title: KPI/SLA framework and performance reporting review
tests.objective: Confirm meaningful efficiency KPIs/SLAs exist, are measured, reported and acted upon.
tests.procedure: Obtain the KPI/SLA definitions and performance reports for each function for Q2 2026. Assess whether metrics cover efficiency (cycle time, cost, throughput, error/rework, backlog), are accurately measured, regularly reported to management, and drive corrective action. Recompute selected KPIs from source data to verify reliability.
tests.controlTested: Performance measurement and management of efficiency (monitoring).
tests.population: KPI/SLA definitions, dashboards and management reports for the four functions, Q2 2026.
tests.sampleBasis: Full review of the KPI suite per function; recomputation of a sample of reported metrics.

tests.title: Resource utilisation and capacity analysis
tests.objective: Assess whether staff and processing capacity are efficiently deployed relative to workload.
tests.procedure: Compare workload volumes to headcount/effort across teams in the four functions for Q2 2026. Identify imbalances — overtime, backlogs, idle capacity, key-person dependencies. Compute productivity ratios (transactions per FTE, cost per transaction) and benchmark across teams/periods. Review use of temporary/overtime resourcing.
tests.controlTested: Efficient deployment of resources (economy/efficiency).
tests.population: Workload volumes, staffing/effort and overtime data for the four functions in Q2 2026.
tests.sampleBasis: Analytical review across all in-scope teams; judgemental focus on teams with backlog or high overtime.

tests.title: Control efficiency / duplication review
tests.objective: Identify duplicated, redundant or disproportionately costly controls that can be streamlined without raising risk.
tests.procedure: Inventory key controls in the selected processes (approvals, reconciliations, checks, reports). Identify overlapping or repeated controls across steps/functions, multiple sign-offs adding little risk reduction, and reconciliations performed in more than one place. Assess each for risk-proportionality and recommend rationalisation while preserving control objectives.
tests.controlTested: Efficiency and proportionality of controls (control rationalisation).
tests.population: Key-control inventory for the selected processes across the four functions.
tests.sampleBasis: Judgemental review of the key controls in each mapped process.

tests.title: Process documentation (SOP) currency and adherence
tests.objective: Confirm processes are supported by current, approved SOPs and executed consistently.
tests.procedure: For each function, confirm SOPs exist, are approved and current, and reflect the actual process. Walk through a sample of transactions against the SOP to test adherence and identify undocumented workarounds. Note where outdated documentation drives inefficiency, inconsistency or training overhead.
tests.controlTested: Standardisation and documentation supporting efficient execution (consistency).
tests.population: SOPs and a sample of executed transactions for the four functions.
tests.sampleBasis: Full review of relevant SOPs; judgemental walkthrough sample per process.

tests.title: Continuous-improvement and analytics maturity assessment
tests.objective: Assess whether functions actively identify, prioritise and implement process improvements using data.
tests.procedure: Review evidence of continuous-improvement activity in Q2 2026 — improvement registers, automation initiatives, post-incident/root-cause actions, and use of data analytics/dashboards. Assess governance over improvement (ownership, tracking to closure) and whether prior identified inefficiencies were addressed. Benchmark maturity against good practice.
tests.controlTested: Continuous-improvement and data-driven management maturity (effectiveness).
tests.population: Improvement registers, automation/initiative records and analytics outputs for the four functions.
tests.sampleBasis: Full review of available improvement records; judgemental assessment of closure of prior inefficiencies.

tests.title: Cost-of-process / value-for-money analysis
tests.objective: Estimate the cost of running each process and identify value-for-money improvement opportunities.
tests.procedure: For a selected process per function, estimate the cost to process (effort, system, rework and delay costs) and unit cost per transaction. Compare across functions/periods and against the value delivered. Quantify the savings potential of the improvement opportunities identified in T2–T8 and prioritise by impact and ease of implementation.
tests.controlTested: Economy and value for money of processes (cost efficiency).
tests.population: Cost, volume and effort data for the selected processes in Q2 2026.
tests.sampleBasis: Judgemental — one representative high-volume process per function, costed end-to-end.

tor.addressee: Head Procurement, Head Risk Management, Head Credit Portfolio, Head Finance
tor.background:
Background and Purpose

This review forms part of the approved risk-based Annual Internal Audit Plan for 2026 and is being conducted in line with the Corporation's drive to improve productivity, reduce cost-to-income and enhance service delivery across its core functions. As CREDICORP scales its lending operations, the efficiency of the processes that support the business — the Credit Portfolio origination-to-collection lifecycle, Procurement (procure-to-pay), Finance (financial close, payments and reporting) and Risk Management — has a direct bearing on customer experience, operating cost and the timeliness of management decision-making. Unlike a conventional controls-assurance review, this audit looks specifically at the economy, efficiency and effectiveness (value-for-money) of these processes, covering the period 1 April to 30 June 2026 (Q2 2026).

The purpose of the audit is to assess how efficiently these four functions operate — examining cycle times and turnaround, levels of manual effort and automation, handoffs and bottlenecks, rework and error rates, duplication of activity, resource utilisation and the management of SLAs/KPIs — and to identify practical, quantified opportunities to streamline, automate and improve without weakening control. On completion, Internal Audit will provide Management and the Board Audit Committee with independent assurance on the operational efficiency and process-improvement maturity of the four functions, together with prioritised, actionable recommendations. We count on the cooperation of process owners and staff in providing timely access to process data, systems and personnel, and we will agree all observations with you before finalising our report.

plan.scope: This process audit covers CREDICORP's end-to-end Procure-to-Pay (P2P) cycle and staff expense management for the period 1 April to 30 June 2026 (Q2 2026). It covers vendor onboarding and master-data maintenance; purchase requisitioning and approval; sourcing/tendering and award; purchase order creation; goods/services receipt; invoice processing and three-way matching; staff expense claims and advances/retirements; payment authorisation and execution; and related general-ledger posting, accruals and reconciliations for the quarter. It also covers compliance with the procurement policy, delegation-of-authority and budgetary controls, and applicable regulatory/tax obligations (e.g. WHT/VAT, CBN/DFI procurement governance). It excludes capital project/major contract management beyond P2P transactional controls, payroll, treasury and bank-funding operations, fixed-asset accounting beyond procurement receipt, and IT general controls except where they directly affect P2P processing. Absent restriction, the review covers all material expense and procurement transactions processed in Q2 2026 across all departments and locations.
objectives: Determine whether purchases and expenses are properly requisitioned, competitively sourced where required, and authorised within the delegation of authority and approved budget before commitment.
Confirm that vendors are legitimate, properly onboarded and that vendor master data (including bank details) is controlled, accurate and free of duplicate or fictitious records.
Assess whether goods and services are received and verified before payment, and that invoices are accurately processed and subject to effective three-way matching.
Evaluate whether payments are valid, accurate, made to the correct payee, properly authorised, and not duplicated.
Determine whether staff expense claims, advances and retirements are valid, supported, within policy, and approved.
Assess segregation of duties across requisition, approval, vendor-master, receipt and payment, and the adequacy of system access.
Confirm compliance with procurement policy, tax/regulatory requirements (WHT/VAT), and accurate, complete recording of expenditure, accruals and reconciliations for the quarter.
keyRisks: Purchases committed without approval, outside delegated authority, or over budget, resulting in unauthorised or wasteful expenditure.
Circumvention of competitive procurement through bid-splitting, inappropriate sole-sourcing, or split purchase orders kept just below approval thresholds.
Fictitious or duplicate (ghost) vendors, or undisclosed related-party/conflict-of-interest vendors, used to divert funds.
Unauthorised changes to vendor bank details (internal or via business-email-compromise) redirecting legitimate payments to fraudulent accounts.
Payment for goods/services not received, short-delivered, or substandard due to weak or non-independent goods-receipt controls.
Inflated, false, or duplicate invoices paid through failure of three-way matching and duplicate-invoice detection.
Duplicate, inaccurate, or unauthorised payments, including manual/emergency payments bypassing standard controls.
Kickbacks/bribery and favouritism in vendor selection and award (corruption risk).
Staff expense claims that are inflated, personal, unsupported, or duplicated, and advances not retired on a timely basis.
Inadequate segregation of duties or excessive system access allowing one person to create a vendor, raise a PO, approve and pay.
Non-deduction/non-remittance of WHT/VAT and inaccurate or incomplete recording of expenditure, accruals and GL postings.
Override or manipulation of approval thresholds and authority limits in the P2P system.

tests.title: Requisition and purchase authorisation within delegated authority and budget
tests.objective: Confirm purchases were requisitioned, approved within the delegation of authority, and within approved budget before commitment.
tests.procedure: From the population of POs/purchases raised in Q2 2026, select a sample. For each, verify an approved requisition exists with business justification, that approval was given at the correct authority level per the DoA matrix before the PO/commitment date, and that the spend was within available budget. Confirm the PO predates the invoice and goods receipt.
tests.controlTested: Authorisation and budgetary control over procurement (authorisation/occurrence).
tests.population: All purchase requisitions/POs raised in Q2 2026.
tests.sampleBasis: Risk-based judgemental/random sample (e.g. 30–40), stratified by value and department, including all high-value and emergency/sole-source purchases.

tests.title: Competitive sourcing and award compliance
tests.objective: Confirm procurements followed competitive/sourcing requirements and that awards were justified and authorised.
tests.procedure: For a sample of awards, verify the required number of quotations/tenders was obtained, evaluation was performed and documented by a tender committee where applicable, and the award was approved. Review sole-source/emergency procurements for documented justification and independent approval. Test for bid-splitting by analysing multiple POs to the same vendor just below thresholds.
tests.controlTested: Competitive procurement and award authorisation (compliance/anti bid-rigging).
tests.population: All awards/POs in Q2 2026 and the vendor-spend transaction listing.
tests.sampleBasis: Judgemental sample of awards above threshold plus analytical scan of 100% of POs for split-purchase patterns.

tests.title: Vendor onboarding and master-data integrity
tests.objective: Confirm vendors are legitimate, properly onboarded, and the vendor master is free of duplicates/fictitious and related-party records.
tests.procedure: Review onboarding for a sample of vendors active in Q2 2026 (CAC, TIN, bank verification, due diligence). Analyse the full vendor master for duplicates (name/TIN/account/address), dormant accounts, and vendor bank accounts matching employee accounts. Screen vendor directors/ownership against employee/related-party data for undisclosed conflicts.
tests.controlTested: Vendor legitimacy and master-data integrity (validity/completeness; anti ghost-vendor).
tests.population: Vendor master file and vendors transacted in Q2 2026; employee master for matching.
tests.sampleBasis: Judgemental sample of new/active vendors plus 100% analytical duplicate/employee-account matching.

tests.title: Vendor bank-detail change control
tests.objective: Confirm changes to vendor bank details are independently verified and authorised under maker-checker.
tests.procedure: Extract vendor bank-detail change logs for Q2 2026. For a sample, confirm an independent, documented verification (e.g. callback to a known contact) and maker-checker authorisation occurred, supported by a valid request. Identify changes made shortly before a payment run and payments made immediately after a detail change.
tests.controlTested: Integrity and authorisation of vendor bank-detail changes (data integrity; anti-BEC/payment diversion).
tests.population: All vendor bank-detail change records in Q2 2026.
tests.sampleBasis: Analytical review of the full change log with judgemental sampling of high-risk changes for authorisation testing.

tests.title: Goods/services receipt verification
tests.objective: Confirm goods/services were received, independently verified, and agree to the order before payment.
tests.procedure: For a sample of payments, trace to a goods/service receipt note (GRN) or service acceptance confirming quantity and specification, completed by someone independent of the requisitioner. Agree GRN to PO and invoice. For services, confirm evidence of delivery/acceptance. Test for invoices paid without a valid receipt.
tests.controlTested: Independent receipt/acceptance of goods and services (occurrence/accuracy).
tests.population: Goods/service receipts and paid invoices for Q2 2026.
tests.sampleBasis: Judgemental sample overlapping payment testing, weighted to high-value and service procurements.

tests.title: Invoice processing and three-way matching
tests.objective: Confirm invoices are accurately processed and subject to effective three-way matching and duplicate detection.
tests.procedure: For a sample of invoices, verify a three-way match (PO, GRN, invoice) on quantity, price and amount within tolerance, with exceptions approved. Recompute invoice totals, taxes and any discounts. Run analytics across the AP population for duplicate invoice numbers, amounts, and same-vendor same-amount/same-date payments.
tests.controlTested: Three-way matching and duplicate-invoice control (accuracy/completeness).
tests.population: All vendor invoices processed in Q2 2026.
tests.sampleBasis: Judgemental sample for match testing plus 100% analytical duplicate-invoice/amount scan.

tests.title: Payment validity, authorisation and accuracy
tests.objective: Confirm payments are valid, correctly authorised, made to the correct payee, and not duplicated.
tests.procedure: From the Q2 2026 payment population, select a sample and trace each payment to an approved, matched invoice and the correct vendor bank account. Verify payment authorisation per the DoA and bank mandate, and that maker/checker were different. Review manual/emergency/urgent payments for justification and approval. Reconcile payments to bank statements and scan for duplicate payments.
tests.controlTested: Payment authorisation, accuracy and validity (authorisation/occurrence; anti duplicate payment).
tests.population: All payments/disbursements processed in Q2 2026.
tests.sampleBasis: Risk-based sample including all high-value and manual/emergency payments plus 100% duplicate-payment analytics.

tests.title: Staff expense claims, advances and retirements
tests.objective: Confirm staff expenses and advances are valid, supported, within policy, approved, and retired on time.
tests.procedure: For a sample of expense claims and advances in Q2 2026, verify valid supporting receipts, business purpose, compliance with expense policy/rates, and approval at the appropriate level. Confirm advances were retired within the policy timeframe and outstanding/unretired advances are followed up. Test for duplicate or personal claims.
tests.controlTested: Validity and policy compliance of expenses/advances (occurrence/accuracy/compliance).
tests.population: All staff expense claims, advances and retirements in Q2 2026.
tests.sampleBasis: Judgemental/random sample stratified by claimant level and value, with review of all long-outstanding advances.

tests.title: Segregation of duties and P2P system access
tests.objective: Confirm no single user can perform conflicting P2P functions and that system access/authority limits are appropriate.
tests.procedure: Obtain P2P system roles/entitlements. Map users across vendor-master maintenance, requisition, approval, goods receipt and payment to identify SoD conflicts. Review users with the ability to both create a vendor and process payment, and those with override/threshold-change rights. Using logs, test a sample of transactions for different maker/checker. Test leavers for timely access removal.
tests.controlTested: Segregation of duties and logical access over P2P (SoD/access control).
tests.population: All P2P user entitlements and the Q2 2026 transaction log.
tests.sampleBasis: Full review of entitlements for conflicts; analytical scan of transactions for same-user conflicts with sample follow-up.

tests.title: Approval-threshold override and split-transaction analytics
tests.objective: Confirm approval thresholds and authority limits are enforced and not circumvented.
tests.procedure: Analyse Q2 2026 requisitions/POs/payments for transactions clustered just below approval thresholds, repeated splits to the same vendor, and use of override/emergency provisions. For a sample of overrides and threshold-edge transactions, confirm justification and senior approval. Review the DoA configuration in the system for accuracy.
tests.controlTested: Enforcement of authority limits and thresholds (authorisation/anti-override).
tests.population: All requisitions, POs and payments in Q2 2026 and system override logs.
tests.sampleBasis: 100% analytical review for threshold-edge/split patterns; judgemental sample of flagged items and overrides.

tests.title: Tax compliance (WHT/VAT) on procurement
tests.objective: Confirm withholding tax and VAT are correctly deducted, accounted for, and remitted on procurement transactions.
tests.procedure: For a sample of vendor payments, recompute WHT and VAT, confirm correct deduction and that VAT was charged by registered vendors. Verify remittance of WHT/VAT to the relevant authority within statutory timelines and that credit notes/receipts are obtained. Identify payments where required deductions were not made.
tests.controlTested: Tax compliance over procurement payments (compliance/accuracy).
tests.population: Vendor payments and tax remittance records for Q2 2026.
tests.sampleBasis: Judgemental sample weighted to high-value and service contracts subject to WHT/VAT.

tests.title: Expenditure recording, accruals and reconciliations
tests.objective: Confirm expenditure is completely and accurately recorded and that AP/accruals and reconciliations are valid for the quarter.
tests.procedure: For a sample of transactions, confirm correct GL account, cost centre, period and amount. Test cut-off around quarter-end for goods/invoices received not recorded (completeness) and amounts recorded early. Review AP and accrual reconciliations for Q2 2026 for preparation, independent review, and clearance of reconciling/aged items.
tests.controlTested: Completeness, accuracy and cut-off of expenditure and reconciliation control (accuracy/completeness).
tests.population: P2P GL postings, AP ledger and accrual reconciliations for Q2 2026.
tests.sampleBasis: Judgemental sample of postings plus full review of quarter-end reconciliations and cut-off testing around 30 June 2026.

fraudRisks.description: Credit/operations staff create loans in the name of fictitious, non-existent, or complicit individuals (or reactivate dormant customers) and disburse funds to accounts they or accomplices control, with no genuine borrower to repay.
fraudRisks.existingControls: KYC/BVN onboarding and credit approval workflow where enforced; core banking (Eazybank) access controls.
fraudRisks.preventionAction: Enforce independent BVN/identity and existence verification before disbursement; segregate loan booking from approval and disbursement; periodic review of new/early-default loans, loans to staff-linked accounts, and disbursements to bank accounts matching staff; data analytics on common addresses/phones/accounts across borrowers.
fraudRisks.owner: Head, Credit Operations / Chief Risk Officer

actions.text: Enforce independent BVN/identity and existence verification before disbursement; segregate loan booking from approval and disbursement; periodic review of new/early-default loans, loans to staff-linked accounts, and disbursements to bank accounts matching staff; data analytics on common addresses/phones/accounts across borrowers.
actions.owner: Head, Credit Operations / Chief Risk Officer

fraudRisks.description: A genuine borrower's approved loan is disbursed to an account controlled by staff (or the customer's bank details are altered before disbursement), redirecting all or part of the funds to a fraudster.
fraudRisks.existingControls: Disbursement instructions and bank-account capture; maker-checker on payments where configured.
fraudRisks.preventionAction: Independently verify and lock beneficiary account (BVN/name match) before disbursement; maker-checker and authorisation independent of loan booking; alert and re-verify on customer bank-detail changes shortly before disbursement; exception report of disbursements to accounts not matching the borrower.

actions.text: Independently verify and lock beneficiary account (BVN/name match) before disbursement; maker-checker and authorisation independent of loan booking; alert and re-verify on customer bank-detail changes shortly before disbursement; exception report of disbursements to accounts not matching the borrower.

fraudRisks.scheme: Disbursement Without/Beyond Credit Approval & Limit Override
fraudRisks.description: Loans are booked and disbursed without the required independent credit-risk approval, in excess of approved amounts/limits, or with manipulated terms, by overriding system controls or exploiting weak segregation of duties.
fraudRisks.existingControls: Delegation-of-authority matrix and approval workflow; system limits where enforced.
fraudRisks.preventionAction: Implement a hard, non-overridable system block preventing disbursement without a valid linked credit-risk approval within delegated authority; restrict and log override/super-user rights; exception reporting reconciling disbursements to approvals; disciplinary action on breaches.
fraudRisks.owner: Chief Risk Officer / Head, Credit Operations

actions.text: Implement a hard, non-overridable system block preventing disbursement without a valid linked credit-risk approval within delegated authority; restrict and log override/super-user rights; exception reporting reconciling disbursements to approvals; disciplinary action on breaches.
actions.owner: Chief Risk Officer / Head, Credit Operations

fraudRisks.description: Staff or borrowers falsify or inflate collateral, income, employment or supporting documentation, or manipulate credit scores/appraisals, to obtain approval for loans that would otherwise be declined.
fraudRisks.existingControls: Documentary verification and credit appraisal standards; independent valuation where required.
fraudRisks.preventionAction: Independent verification of income/employment and collateral (third-party valuation, registry checks); QA review of a sample of approved files; analytics on high override/high-exception approvers; segregation between appraisal and approval.
fraudRisks.owner: Chief Risk Officer / Head, Credit Risk

actions.text: Independent verification of income/employment and collateral (third-party valuation, registry checks); QA review of a sample of approved files; analytics on high override/high-exception approvers; segregation between appraisal and approval.

processReviews.summary: This is the CREDICORP Internal Audit SOP (presented here untitled/unspecified business unit, but its content is wholly the Internal Audit Function's procedures). It is comprehensive and broadly aligned to the IIA Global Internal Audit Standards (GIAS), covering the full assurance lifecycle (annual and engagement planning, execution, reporting, exception management), investigations, whistleblowing, regulatory returns, IS reviews, VFM, advisory engagements with explicit independence safeguards, annual declarations, self-assessment, and a defined SOP-review cycle. Strong practices are embedded: risk-based planning, the 5C/CCCER findings model, a central issues repository, the contradictory (right-of-reply) procedure, defined SLAs/KPIs, independence declarations and 7-year retention. However, effectiveness is undermined by a foundational governance gap — the approval block is unsigned and the revision history is blank, so the SOP is not evidenced as formally approved or version-controlled (and the document is effectively untitled/unbranded). The most material systemic weakness is heavy concentration of duties in the Head, Internal Audit (HIA), who in several procedures prepares, reviews and approves the same work and personally leads investigations/whistleblowing, weakening segregation of duties and independent review. Further gaps: QA performed by the HIA over the HIA's own work; an optional (not mandatory) peer review and no defined External Quality Assessment (EQA) cycle; no deputy/acting-HIA arrangement; reliance on manual trackers and shared-drive filing; unbounded investigation timelines; and minor numbering/timeline inconsistencies. Addressing these would move the function from Adequate to Strong.

findings.title: SOP not evidenced as approved or version-controlled (and untitled)
findings.detail: The Approval block (Document Owner, Reviewed/Checked by, Approved by) is blank/unsigned and undated, and the Revision History table is entirely empty; the document is presented without a clear title/business-unit identification. Section 6.16 requires MD approval of the SOP, but no evidence of approval or versioning is present.
findings.recommendation: Title and identify the document clearly (Internal Audit SOP, owning function, document reference), complete the approval block with names, signatures and dates (preparer, independent reviewer, MD/CEO approver), and populate the revision history (version, date, summary of changes). Apply formal version control going forward.

findings.title: Concentration of duties in the HIA (prepare–review–approve)
findings.detail: Across multiple procedures the HIA both performs/owns and approves the same activity — sole preparer and approver of annual plan inputs; in investigations (6.06) the HIA reviews case files, investigates and signs the final report; in whistleblowing (6.07) the HIA receives, triages, leads the investigation team and reports. The HIA is also document owner, preparer and within the SOP approval chain. This weakens segregation of duties and independent challenge.
findings.recommendation: Introduce independent checkpoints: route HIA-prepared deliverables (plan, self-assessment, HIA-led investigations) to the BAC Chair or an independent reviewer for approval; mandate explicit BAC-Chair oversight for any matter implicating the HIA; and define a deputy/acting-HIA to act where the HIA is conflicted or unavailable.

findings.title: Limited independent QA over HIA-performed work
findings.detail: QA review in reporting (6.04 step 7) and advisory (6.14 step 8) is performed by the HIA. Where the HIA personally prepares or leads work, there is no independent second-line review, creating self-review risk. The self-assessment peer review (6.13 step 5) is marked 'Optional'.
findings.recommendation: Define an independent QA mechanism for HIA-originated work (peer review, co-source partner, or BAC-directed reviewer). Make periodic independent/peer review mandatory and establish an External Quality Assessment (EQA) at least once every five years per IIA GIAS.

findings.title: No defined External Quality Assessment (EQA) cycle
findings.detail: Section 6.13 covers annual internal self-assessment but the SOP does not mandate a five-yearly external quality assessment by a qualified independent assessor, a GIAS requirement.
findings.recommendation: Add a procedure requiring an EQA at least every five years (or self-assessment with independent validation), with results reported to the Board through the BAC.

findings.title: No succession / delegation when HIA is unavailable or conflicted
findings.detail: Almost every procedure assigns final responsibility to the HIA, but there is no defined acting/delegate arrangement for absence, vacancy or conflict of interest (beyond the partial whistleblowing carve-out). This is a continuity and independence risk.
findings.recommendation: Define a formal delegation-of-authority and acting-HIA arrangement (senior auditor or BAC-designated party), including how approvals and reporting continue when the HIA is unavailable or conflicted.

findings.title: Investigation timelines aspirational and not consistently bounded
findings.detail: 6.06 commits only to 'endeavour' to complete investigations within two weeks and explicitly notes no fixed timeframe; escalation triggers and status-update cadence for prolonged or complex investigations are not defined.
findings.recommendation: Define target timelines by case severity, a status-update cadence to the MD/CEO/BAC where the target is exceeded, and explicit escalation triggers.

findings.title: Minor numbering and timeline inconsistencies
findings.detail: Section 6.04 skips step 2 (numbered 1, 3, 4...). In 6.09 step 5 the timing reads 'Before the end of the first week after the month Within the first five (5) days of the month' (conflicting phrasing). Several IS reviews (6.10) and VFM (6.11) lack defined reporting timelines/SLAs that exist elsewhere; 6.04 also has a potential sequencing tension (management response 'before closing meeting' yet draft report prepared after it).
findings.recommendation: Correct step numbering in 6.04, resolve the conflicting deadline wording in 6.09 step 5, clarify the 6.04 response/closing-meeting sequence, and standardise reporting timelines/SLAs across all sub-procedures including IS reviews and VFM.

findings.title: Reliance on manual trackers and shared-drive filing
findings.detail: Issues tracking, planning, workpaper management and follow-up rely on spreadsheets/templates, OneDrive folders and Microsoft Forms. This is manual, prone to version and cross-referencing error, and limits real-time reporting of issue ageing and trends.
findings.recommendation: Adopt audit management/GRC software to automate the audit lifecycle, issues tracking and ageing, automated reminders, and dashboard reporting to MANCO/BAC, integrated with the document repository for controlled workpaper management.

findings.title: Manual, calendar-driven follow-up and reminders
findings.detail: Exception follow-up (6.05) depends on manually sent monthly reminders, risking missed reminders and inconsistent escalation as issue volumes grow.
findings.recommendation: Automate reminder generation and severity-based escalation within the tracking tool, with exception-ageing dashboards and auto-escalation of overdue high/critical items to the BAC.

findings.title: Overlapping TOR amendment and dissemination steps
findings.detail: In 6.02, steps 7–10 separately prepare, communicate, amend, re-approve and re-disseminate the TOR, and the TOR also serves as the opening-meeting agenda (step 13). For low-complexity engagements this multi-pass cycle is repetitive and time-consuming.
findings.recommendation: Introduce a risk-tiered/streamlined TOR process for routine engagements (single combined draft-amend-approve cycle), reserving the full multi-step process for complex or co-sourced audits.

findings.title: Comprehensive, standards-aligned coverage
findings.detail: The SOP maps to GIAS and CBN/AML-CFT requirements and covers the full lifecycle plus investigations, whistleblowing, regulatory returns, IS reviews, VFM, advisory (with explicit independence safeguards in 6.15), annual declarations and self-assessment — a notably complete framework.
findings.recommendation: Maintain coverage and keep mapping current to the latest GIAS and CBN guidance at each biennial review.

findings.title: Strong findings discipline, SLAs and independence safeguards
findings.detail: Use of the 5C/CCCER findings model with root-cause analysis, a central issues repository, the contradictory (right-of-reply) procedure, a defined SLA/KPI table, quarterly independence confirmation, annual declarations (incl. 40-hour CPD) and 7-year retention reflect mature, measurable practice.
findings.recommendation: Preserve these controls and report SLA/KPI performance to the BAC to demonstrate ongoing conformance.

keyRecommendations: Formally title, approve, sign, date and version-control the SOP, and maintain a populated revision history.

Address concentration of duties in the HIA by introducing independent review/approval (BAC Chair or designated reviewer) for HIA-prepared plans, self-assessments, and HIA-led/conflicted investigations and whistleblowing cases.
Establish mandatory independent/peer QA and an External Quality Assessment at least every five years in line with IIA GIAS.
Define a formal delegation/acting-HIA arrangement for absence, vacancy or conflict of interest.
Invest in audit management/GRC tooling to automate the audit lifecycle, issues ageing, reminders and BAC/MANCO dashboard reporting.
Bound investigation timelines by severity with escalation triggers, and correct the minor numbering/timeline inconsistencies (6.04, 6.09) and standardise SLAs across all sub-procedures.

processReviews.summary: The document is a well-written Corporate Communications Policy that comprehensively covers principles, scope, legal/regulatory alignment (including NDPA 2023), spokespersonship, branding, crisis communication, roles, consequences of non-compliance and a review cycle. As a policy it is largely sound and reads professionally. However, assessed as an operating procedure (SOP) for the Corporate Communications business unit it is incomplete: it sets standards but does not translate them into executable process. There is no step-by-step content clearance/approval workflow, no defined turnaround times/SLAs (e.g. for media enquiries, press releases, social posts, crisis response), no RACI/approval matrix, no escalation trigger levels with named roles, and no monitoring metrics despite the policy referencing evaluation and monitoring. Governance hygiene is also incomplete — the effective date, next review date, version-history table and approval/signature table are all blank, so the policy is not evidenced as formally approved or version-controlled. There is a naming inconsistency between 'Head, Corporate Communications', 'Communications Department' and 'Strategic Communications' that blurs ownership. Addressing these — principally by issuing a companion SOP with workflows, timelines and an approval matrix, and by executing document control — would raise effectiveness materially.

findings.title: Policy not evidenced as approved or version-controlled
findings.detail: Effective Date and Next Review Date are blank; the Document Control/Version History table and the Approval/Signature table are entirely empty. The policy therefore has no evidence of formal approval, ownership sign-off or version control.
findings.recommendation: Complete the document-control block (effective date, next review date), populate the version history (version, date, change, prepared/reviewed/approved by), and obtain signed, dated approval (preparer, reviewer, MD/CEO or delegated authority) before the policy is relied upon.

findings.title: No content clearance / approval workflow
findings.detail: The policy states that approvals 'where required' and coordination will apply, but nowhere defines the actual approval workflow — who drafts, who reviews (e.g. Legal/Compliance/Risk), who approves, and at what content type/risk level — before internal or external communication is released.
findings.recommendation: Add a content-approval matrix and workflow specifying required reviewers and approvers by communication type (press release, social media, regulatory/public statement, beneficiary comms), including mandatory Legal/Compliance review for regulatory or sensitive content, with a clear maker-checker sequence.

findings.title: No defined timelines / SLAs and turnaround standards
findings.detail: The policy repeatedly requires 'timeliness' and 'responsiveness' but sets no measurable turnaround times for media enquiries, approval of materials, social-media response, or crisis acknowledgement/first-statement, leaving 'timely' undefined and unmanageable.
findings.recommendation: Define SLAs (e.g. media enquiry acknowledgement within X hours, crisis holding statement within Y hours, routine approval within Z working days) in a companion SOP, and track performance against them.

findings.title: Crisis communication lacks an escalation matrix and named roles
findings.detail: Section 11 sets sound principles and central coordination but does not define severity tiers, escalation triggers, a crisis team composition, notification timelines, or who approves messaging at each level — it says 'designated authority channels' without naming them.
findings.recommendation: Add a crisis escalation matrix with severity levels, a standing crisis-communications team (roles/named positions incl. MD/CEO, Legal, Risk), notification and approval timelines, and pre-cleared holding-statement templates.

findings.title: Inconsistent ownership naming
findings.detail: The document refers variously to 'Head, Corporate Communications', 'Communications Department', 'Head of Communications Department' and 'Strategic Communications' (Sections 12–13) for implementation and ownership, creating ambiguity about the accountable function.
findings.recommendation: Standardise on a single defined function/role title throughout and confirm it in the roles-and-responsibilities section to remove ambiguity over accountability.

findings.title: No monitoring metrics or defined compliance-monitoring mechanism
findings.detail: Sections 5 and 12 reference evaluation and monitoring of compliance, but no KPIs, measurement methods, reporting cadence or responsible monitor are specified, so 'monitoring and compliance' cannot be evidenced.
findings.recommendation: Define communication KPIs (e.g. approval SLA adherence, media-enquiry response time, brand-compliance exceptions, crisis-response time) and a periodic compliance-monitoring and reporting routine to management.

findings.title: No records management / retention provision
findings.detail: The policy governs communication assets and content but does not address retention, archiving or storage of communication records (approvals, press releases, media logs, crisis logs), unlike other CREDICORP SOPs which specify retention.
findings.recommendation: Add a records-management clause specifying what communication records are retained, where, and for how long (aligned to the Corporation's retention standard), including an auditable log of approvals and public statements.

findings.title: Policy not paired with an executable SOP / templates
findings.detail: The document is a principles-level policy without the operational procedures, checklists and templates needed for day-to-day execution (e.g. press-release checklist, social-media calendar/approval flow, media-enquiry log, brand-asset request form).
findings.recommendation: Develop a companion Corporate Communications SOP with process flows, RACI, and standard templates/checklists, and consider a workflow tool for content requests, approvals and tracking to reduce manual coordination.

findings.title: Social media and digital governance under-specified
findings.detail: Digital and social platforms are listed as channels, but there is no specific governance for account ownership, posting/approval rights, monitoring, or handling of user comments/complaints on social media — a high-velocity reputational channel.
findings.recommendation: Add a digital/social-media governance section covering account custodianship, posting and approval rights, community-management/response rules, and monitoring, integrated with the IT and NDPA requirements.

findings.title: Comprehensive, well-structured coverage
findings.detail: The policy covers purpose, scope, legal/regulatory compliance (incl. NDPA 2023), goals/objectives, guiding principles, audiences, channels, spokespersonship, branding, crisis communication, roles, and review — a thorough and coherent framework.
findings.recommendation: Maintain this coverage and keep it aligned to evolving regulatory and reputational requirements at each review.

findings.title: Strong spokespersonship and non-compliance controls
findings.detail: Clear designation of the MD/CEO as principal spokesperson, explicit restriction on unauthorised communication across all platforms, central coordination of public statements, and a detailed, graduated set of consequences for non-compliance (including third-party contractual sanctions) are notable control strengths.
findings.recommendation: Preserve these controls and operationalise them via the authorisation workflow and a spokesperson-designation log.

findings.title: Defined review cycle and brand governance
findings.detail: A biennial (2-year or earlier) review requirement, controlled amendment/approval process, and clear brand ownership/visual-identity governance provide good policy-maintenance and reputational-asset protection.
findings.recommendation: Once document control is completed, adhere to the review cycle and record each review outcome in the version history.

keyRecommendations: Execute document control: set effective/next-review dates, populate the version history, and obtain signed, dated approval by the appropriate authority.

Issue a companion Corporate Communications SOP that converts the policy into executable workflows, with a content approval/clearance matrix and mandatory Legal/Compliance review for regulatory or sensitive content.
Define measurable turnaround SLAs for media enquiries, content approvals, social-media response and crisis communication.
Add a crisis-communication escalation matrix with severity tiers, named crisis-team roles, notification/approval timelines and pre-cleared holding-statement templates.
Establish communication KPIs and a periodic compliance-monitoring and reporting routine, plus a records-retention clause and social/digital governance.
Standardise the owning-function title throughout to remove ambiguity between 'Corporate Communications' and 'Strategic Communications'.

iaSA.commentary: In our opinion the CREDICORP internal audit function Partially Conforms to the Global Internal Audit Standards (2024) at this early stage, with an overall maturity of approximately 2.5 (Developing-to-Established) — a credible position for a function established only in FY2025. Key strengths are a competent and qualified Head of Internal Audit, a comprehensive risk-based methodology, sound engagement planning and conduct (5C findings, root-cause analysis, action plans), functional reporting to the Board Audit Committee, and a well-articulated Charter/SOP. Priority non-conformances concentrate in Board oversight and quality (Principles 8 and 12): insufficient resourcing and key-person dependency (8.2, 10.2), absence of a functioning Quality Assurance and Improvement Programme (8.3, 12.1), no External Quality Assessment yet performed (8.4), and an SOP not yet formally approved/version-controlled — alongside the need to ratify the mandate/Charter through the now fully constituted Board. A five-yearly external quality assessment is not yet due but should be formally scheduled and completed within five years of the function's establishment (target 2029), preceded by completion of recruitment, a QAIP, a multi-year strategy, and investment in audit-management/GRC tooling.

1.notes: Integrity is well anchored in the Charter/SOP and Code of Ethics; embedding through engagements is still maturing.

2.notes: Objectivity mechanisms exist but are constrained by the single-person structure and absence of independent review.
2.action: Document objectivity safeguards: disclose impairments to the BAC and obtain independent/co-sourced review of advisory work that is later subject to assurance.

3.notes: Strong HIA competence but narrow bench, key-person dependency and unproven CPD cycle pending recruitment.
3.action: Perform a competency/skills-gap assessment; secure co-sourcing for specialist areas and a structured annual training plan.

4.notes: Due care and skepticism are embedded in methodology; a conformance basis (QAIP) is not yet established.
4.action: Concentrate effort on high-risk coverage and use co-sourcing to maintain depth where capacity is constrained.

5.notes: Confidentiality is well defined; secure-storage/access controls over workpapers need strengthening.

6.notes: Mandate and Charter exist but require formal ratification by a fully constituted Board.
6.action: Review the charter annually and reaffirm it with the Board.

7.notes: Functional reporting to the BAC and a qualified HIA give sound independence positioning.

8.notes: Board oversight of resources, quality and EQA is the weakest area — resourcing, QAIP and EQA are not yet in place.
8.action: Formalise periodic private (executive) sessions between the Head, IA and the BAC.

9.notes: Risk-based annual planning is a clear strength; a formal multi-year strategy and reliance framework are missing.
9.action: Develop a multi-year IA strategy and reflect resource constraints/coverage gaps explicitly in the plan presented to the BAC.

10.notes: Resource management is constrained — understaffed, budget-limited and lacking GRC/analytics tooling.
10.action: Present a resourcing business case to the BAC for additional staff and/or formal co-sourcing, plus budget for tools and training; monitor resource adequacy against the plan.

11.notes: Reporting and communication practices are well designed; risk-acceptance escalation and error-correction protocols need adding.
11.action: Formalise a communication protocol (report format, timeliness, escalation) and report IA performance metrics to the BAC.

12.notes: Quality programme is largely absent — QAIP, performance measurement and independent oversight not yet operational.
12.action: Establish a documented QAIP (ongoing + periodic internal assessments) and schedule an external quality assessment within five years.

13.notes: Engagement planning is robust (TOR, risk assessment, work programs); evaluation-criteria agreement can be tightened.
13.action: Standardise engagement-planning templates and risk/control matrices across all engagements.

14.notes: Engagement conduct is a strength — strong evidence, 5C findings, root cause and action plans; minor gaps in formal conclusions.
14.action: Strengthen working-paper and evidence standards; obtain independent or co-sourced review on complex/high-risk engagements.

15.notes: Results communication and follow-up are defined; monitoring effectiveness depends on automation still to be implemented.
15.action: Maintain a complete issue-tracking log with ageing and overdue escalation to the BAC, and verify closures with evidence.

1.1.evidence: IA Charter/SOP require honesty, objectivity and due professional care; HIA is a chartered professional bound by IIA Code of Ethics.

1.2.evidence: SOP references CREDICORP values and Code of Ethics; annual declaration attests conformance to organisational values.
1.2.gap: Organisation's ethical expectations not yet demonstrably tested/embedded through IA engagements given nascent stage.
1.2.action: Incorporate assessment of organisational ethics/tone-at-the-top into the audit plan and document IA's own alignment.

1.3.evidence: SOP mandates compliance with laws/regulations (CBN, NDPA) and IIA Code of Ethics; whistleblowing route defined.

2.1.evidence: Pre-engagement individual independence disclosures required; annual declaration covers conflicts of interest.
2.1.gap: Single-person function limits demonstrable individual objectivity on areas the HIA may have influenced.
2.1.action: On recruitment, allocate engagements to avoid self-review; use co-source for HIA-conflicted areas.

2.2.evidence: SOP provides for reassignment where conflicts identified and advisory safeguards (6.15).
2.2.gap: No independent QA/deputy to safeguard objectivity over HIA-performed work; single-person structure.
2.2.action: Recruit staff and establish independent/peer review and BAC-Chair oversight for HIA-conflicted work.

2.3.evidence: Engagement-level and annual declarations disclose impairments to HIA/BAC Chair; escalation path defined.

3.1.evidence: HIA is an experienced qualified professional; SOP requires competent execution to professional standards.
3.1.gap: Function lacks breadth of competencies (IT/IS, data analytics, credit) pending recruitment; key-person dependency.
3.1.action: Complete recruitment of IT/IS and financial/ops auditors; maintain a competency/skills matrix and use co-sourcing for specialist areas.

3.2.evidence: SOP mandates minimum 40 hours CPD per auditor per year, attested in annual declaration.
3.2.gap: CPD tracking not yet evidenced across a full cycle for a new team.
3.2.action: Maintain CPD logs and a training plan aligned to the audit universe; report CPD attainment to BAC annually.

4.1.evidence: SOP and Charter reference conformance with IIA Global Internal Audit Standards.
4.1.gap: No QAIP or EQA yet performed to substantiate a conformance statement.
4.1.action: Establish QAIP with internal assessments and commission first EQA within five years.

4.2.evidence: Risk-based methodology, 5C/CCCER findings model, supervisory review of fieldwork embedded in SOP.

4.3.evidence: SOP requires evidence-based findings, corroboration and management-response revalidation.

5.1.evidence: SOP classifies audit records confidential, restricts use to official purposes; NDPA referenced.

5.2.evidence: Records held in OneDrive with confidentiality classification and 7-year retention.

extFindings.title: Insufficient personnel / key-person dependency in Finance & Accounts
extFindings.detail: The CFO is the only dedicated senior member of the finance unit, supported by cross-functional staff, and is responsible for overseeing and leading most or all critical financial processes and controls.
extFindings.risk: High dependency on a single individual increases the risk of errors, omissions and fraud due to limited independent review or segregation of duties; the CFO's absence or unavailability could disrupt the finance function and impair timely, accurate financial reporting.
extFindings.recommendation: Strengthen the finance unit by permanently transferring supporting staff to finance, or recruiting/training additional qualified personnel, to ensure adequate segregation of duties, support the CFO and enhance the resilience and effectiveness of the function.

extFindings.title: CBN operating licence not yet secured (Approval-in-Principle only)
extFindings.detail: The Corporation had not obtained a full CBN operating licence (holding only an approval in principle, which does not permit full regulated operations) and was operating under the Bank of Industry's licence via a fund-management arrangement. The full wholesale DFI licence was subsequently approved by CBN on 26 November 2025.
extFindings.risk: Operating without a full CBN licence exposes the Corporation to regulatory risk.
extFindings.recommendation: Expedite efforts to obtain the full CBN licence and regularly review regulatory developments to ensure readiness for full compliance upon licensing.

extFindings.title: Absence of an IFRS 9 impairment (ECL) model for the loan portfolio
extFindings.detail: No formal impairment model had been developed or implemented for the loan portfolio; instead an interim flat provision of 2% of the portfolio was applied, with no structured process for timely identification, measurement and recognition of expected credit losses.
extFindings.risk: Non-compliance with IFRS 9 (expected credit losses) risking inaccurate financial statements and regulatory penalties; potential misstatement of credit losses undermining reporting reliability; and weak risk management from lack of early detection of deteriorating exposures.
extFindings.recommendation: Promptly develop and implement an IFRS 9-compliant impairment model that segments loans by risk, sets criteria for significant increase in credit risk, and computes ECL using historical, current and forward-looking data, with regular review, clear documentation, assigned responsibilities and staff training for consistent application.

extFindings.title: Absence of an Internal Audit function and formal internal controls
extFindings.detail: No established internal audit function and a lack of formal internal controls across key operational areas such as financial reporting and compliance monitoring; regulatory compliance was driven by the Legal department with all compliance checks performed by the same staff member.
extFindings.risk: Limits the ability to independently assess and improve risk management, internal controls and governance, increasing the risk that errors, fraud or control weaknesses go undetected and affecting the reliability of financial reporting and operational efficiency.
extFindings.recommendation: Establish an internal audit function to provide assurance to management and those charged with governance on the adequacy and effectiveness of internal controls and risk management processes.

extFindings.title: Weak internal control environment
extFindings.detail: Weaknesses identified in the internal control environment, specifically inadequate segregation of duties and lack of timely reconciliations.
extFindings.risk: Weak internal controls increase the risk of undetected errors, fraud and misstatements, potentially resulting in inaccurate financial reporting, financial losses and non-compliance with applicable laws and regulations.
extFindings.recommendation: Review and strengthen the internal control environment, including implementing appropriate segregation of duties, enhancing review, ensuring timely reconciliations, and providing regular staff training on internal control procedures.

extFindings.title: Late remittance of statutory deductions (PAYE and Pension)
extFindings.detail: PAYE and Pension deductions were made from payments to suppliers and employees but none were remitted to the appropriate government agencies during the period under review; noted across multiple transactions and payroll cycles.
extFindings.risk: Failure to remit statutory deductions exposes the Corporation to penalties, interest charges and potential legal action, reputational damage and additional scrutiny from tax and regulatory bodies.
extFindings.recommendation: Remit all statutory deductions (PAYE, Pension) promptly and in full; establish robust internal controls and monitoring to track deductions and remittances; regularly review statutory compliance requirements and train responsible staff; and engage the relevant authorities to resolve any outstanding liabilities.

extFindings.title: Omission of dates on signed approval documents
extFindings.detail: Although approvals and supporting documentation were generally present and appropriately authorised, signatures on several key documents (contracts, approval forms, financial records) were not accompanied by the date of signing — a recurring issue in the first year of operation.
extFindings.risk: Absence of dates impedes establishing a clear timeline of events, weakening the audit trail and complicating audits, investigations and reviews, and making it difficult to hold individuals accountable for timely approvals.
extFindings.recommendation: Establish and enforce a formal policy requiring all signatures on official documents to be accompanied by the date of signing, supported by staff communication, updated document templates, training and periodic compliance reviews.

extFindings.title: Non-implementation of Internal Control Over Financial Reporting (ICFR)
extFindings.detail: The entity has not implemented Internal Control Over Financial Reporting in line with the regulations and guidance issued by the Financial Reporting Council of Nigeria (FRCN Act 2023, pursuant to Sections 72(f) and 50 of the Financial Reporting Act 2011 as amended), which require management of Public Interest Entities (PIEs) to assess and report on the effectiveness of their internal controls over financial reporting, including information systems controls, with external auditors providing an attestation.
extFindings.risk: Risk that a deficiency, significant deficiency or material weakness exists in management's internal controls; risk of non-compliance with regulatory requirements exposing the company to fines and penalties; and exposure to reputational and regulatory risk and potential financial loss due to sanctions from the regulator.
extFindings.recommendation: Management should implement Internal Control Over Financial Reporting in accordance with the guidelines issued by the FRCN to prevent or detect material misstatements and deficiencies in the internal controls established by management.
extFindings.owner: Management (Risk, Internal Control, Finance and Internal Audit project team)

extFindings.title: Inability to back-post accounting journals to closed periods
extFindings.detail: The accounting software in use does not permit the posting of journals to closed accounting periods. As a result, certain journal entries relating to the 2024 financial year — including audit adjustments — were posted in 2025, the subsequent financial year. This prevents transactions and adjustments from being recorded in the appropriate accounting period and results in timing differences between the period to which items relate and the period in which they are recorded in the general ledger.
extFindings.risk: Increases the risk of misstatement of financial information (income, expenses, assets or liabilities recorded in the wrong period); inaccurate period-end financial reporting affecting the reliability of management accounts and audited financial statements; and difficulty ensuring audit adjustments are promptly and correctly reflected, impacting audit conclusions and comparability between periods.
extFindings.recommendation: Management should review the current system's limitations and either (i) ensure the accounting system allows controlled back-posting of journals to closed periods, subject to appropriate authorisation and audit-trail controls, or (ii) establish a robust workaround whereby all audit adjustments and prior-period journals are passed immediately with clear documentation and management approval; and strengthen period-end and year-end close procedures to ensure all necessary adjustments are identified and recorded before finalisation and system closure.
extFindings.owner: Management (Finance, with IT and Strategy teams)

extFindings.title: Non-compliance with fee and commission payment terms under the BOI Disbursement Agreement
extFindings.detail: The entity entered into an agreement with the Bank of Industry (BOI) to facilitate disbursement of funds to Participating Financial Institutions (PFIs), under which a fee and commission expense is chargeable on every disbursement. During the year, although multiple disbursements were made to PFIs, the entity paid the related fee and commission only twice and then ceased further payments. No formal documentation, contractual amendment, management approval or written waiver from BOI was obtained to support the discontinuation; management explained the cessation was based on verbal understanding and informal communication, with no written confirmation or evidence provided.
extFindings.risk: Absence of formal documentation exposes the entity to risk of unrecorded or understated liabilities and expenses, potentially causing material misstatement of the financial statements; risk of breach of contractual obligations leading to disputes, penalties or retrospective claims by BOI; and increased litigation and reputational risk from reliance on informal, undocumented agreements.
extFindings.recommendation: Ensure all contractual obligations, including fees and commissions payable, are clearly understood, consistently applied and fully documented. Specifically, obtain formal written confirmation or an amendment to the agreement from BOI where any change to the fee/commission structure or payment terms has been agreed, and implement periodic reviews of major contracts to ensure ongoing compliance with agreed terms.
